reconcile.connective: Defenders answer that the infant imagery is a translation artifact: the chronology makes Ishmael about seventeen, so only the provisions, not the boy, sat on Hagar's shoulder.

discrepancy.connective: John Skinner's critical commentary presses the source-critical objection: the expulsion narrative treats Ishmael as a small child carried and cast down, and so does not appear to know the Priestly chronology of 16:16 and 21:5 that would make him a teenager.

skeptic.name: John Skinner
skeptic.work: A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on Genesis (International Critical Commentary)
skeptic.attribution: John Skinner (d. 1925), A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on Genesis, ICC (1910)

excerpts.excerpt_text: What adds to the appearance of cruelty in this case is, that our translation seems to represent Ishmael as being a young child; and that Hagar was obliged to carry him, the bread, and the bottle of water on her back or shoulder at the same time. But that Ishmael could not be carried on his mother's shoulder will be sufficiently evident when his age is considered … we shall find that Ishmael was at the time of his leaving Abraham not less than seventeen years old …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly names the infant-imagery problem ('our translation seems to represent Ishmael as being a young child') and the shoulder-carrying difficulty, then resolves it by computing his age at ~17 — the strongest single harmonization on the row.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), on Genesis 21:14
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke addresses this passage directly: he raises the 'appearance of cruelty' created by the infant-child reading and answers it by computing Ishmael's age (born when Abraham was 86, Isaac when he was 100, plus Isaac's weaning), concluding Ishmael was about seventeen and walked rather than was carried.
